legal_002:n1.prompt:
You are helping me conduct a preliminary trademark search before I file a trademark application with the USPTO. 

First, ask me for: (1) the exact company/brand name and any logo text or slogan I want to trademark, (2) a description of the goods/services this mark covers (or the general industry, e.g., 'software', 'coffee shop', 'consulting'), and (3) any known competitor or similar brand names I'm already worried about.

Once I provide this, use the USPTO Trademark Search System (TMSearch) at https://tmsearch.uspto.gov/search/search-information to search for existing registered or pending trademarks that could conflict with mine. Search using: the exact mark name, close phonetic/spelling variants, and the mark combined with relevant keywords from the goods/services description. Also check the appropriate Nice Classification class(es) that best match my goods/services.

For each search, record: the conflicting mark name, its registration/serial number, status (registered, pending, abandoned, cancelled), owner, filing date, and the goods/services class it covers. Note how similar each result is to my mark (identical, phonetically similar, visually similar, or same/adjacent class).

Done looks like: a clear written summary listing (a) any exact or near-identical matches found, (b) any similar marks in the same or related classes, (c) an overall risk assessment (low/medium/high likelihood of conflict), and (d) a recommendation on whether to proceed, modify the mark, or consult a trademark attorney before filing.

Report back with this summary in plain text, including direct links to any conflicting USPTO records you found, so I can review the findings myself.

legal_002:n2.prompt:
You are helping me determine the correct USPTO trademark filing class(es) (Nice Classification) for our company name and/or logo before we submit a trademark application. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the exact company/brand name and, if applicable, the logo image or description, (2) our domain, (3) a plain-language description of the goods and/or services we sell or plan to sell, and (4) whether we want to protect the wordmark, the logo, or both.

Using that information, do the following: (a) search the USPTO's Trademark ID Manual and the free TESS (Trademark Electronic Search System) database on the USPTO website to identify which of the 45 international (Nice) classes match our goods/services — note both the class number(s) and the standardized identification-of-goods/services language from the ID Manual that most closely fits what we offer; (b) run a knockout search in TESS for our proposed name/logo within those classes to flag any identical or highly similar existing marks that could pose a conflict; (c) if our offerings span multiple classes (e.g., software plus consulting services), list each relevant class separately with its matching goods/services description, since each additional class typically increases filing cost.

Done looks like: a written summary listing (1) each recommended Nice class number, (2) the exact standardized description text pulled from the ID Manual for that class, (3) any potential conflicting marks found in TESS with their serial/registration numbers, and (4) a note on which classes are essential now versus optional for future expansion. Report this summary back to me in a clear list so I can review before we proceed to actually filing the application.

legal_002:n3.prompt:
You are helping me draft the goods/services description for a USPTO trademark application (this is preparation only — the actual filing and any USPTO fees/submission remain separate steps requiring my sign-off). 

If you don't already have it from me, ask for: (1) my company/brand name and, if applicable, a description or image reference of the logo being trademarked; (2) a plain-language summary of what my business actually sells or does today, plus any products/services planned within the next 6-12 months; (3) my website domain, if I have one, so you can review it for context on offerings.

Using this information, please: 
1. Research how the USPTO's Trademark ID Manual classifies similar goods/services, and identify the likely International Class(es) (e.g., Class 9 for software, Class 35 for business services, Class 42 for SaaS) that fit my business. 
2. Draft 2-3 candidate goods/services descriptions per relevant class, written in the precise, USPTO-acceptable style (specific, not overly broad, avoiding vague terms like 'services' alone). 
3. Note tradeoffs: broader descriptions offer more protection but face higher rejection risk; narrower descriptions are safer but limit coverage. 
4. Flag any additional classes I may want to consider based on my stated future plans. 
5. Compile everything into a single document or summary showing: recommended class(es), draft description text for each, and your reasoning. 

Done means I have a clear, ready-to-review draft with alternative phrasings and class recommendations, plus a short explanation of tradeoffs. 

Report back with the full draft document, your class recommendations, and any open questions needing my input (e.g., ambiguity about future product lines). Do not submit anything to the USPTO or finalize the description — stop for human sign-off before any filing action is taken.

legal_002:n4.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for and track an IP attorney's trademark clearance review before we file with the USPTO. The actual legal analysis (likelihood-of-confusion assessment and classification judgment) remains a human step that only a licensed IP attorney can perform — please do not attempt that analysis yourself.

First, ask me for anything you need that's missing: our company/brand name, logo file(s) or description, the goods/services we offer, our target USPTO classes (if we have a guess), any prior trademark search results we've already gathered, and the attorney's or law firm's contact email if we already have one engaged.

Then do the following prep work:
1. Draft a clear, organized email to our IP attorney requesting a clearance review, summarizing the mark (word mark and/or logo), the goods/services description, and any classification guess.
2. Compile a checklist of documents/info the attorney will likely need: specimen of use, first-use dates, prior search results, business description, and any known competitor marks we're aware of.
3. Prepare a tracking log (simple table) with columns for: date sent, attorney name, status, expected response date, and outcome — so we can monitor this async request.
4. Note in the log that this request is now pending and must be polled/checked periodically since the attorney's analysis will land later, not immediately.

Once the email draft, document checklist, and tracking log are ready, present them to me and stop for human sign-off before anything is sent to the attorney. Do not send the email, submit any filing, or make legal judgments about confusion risk or classification yourself.

Report back with: the drafted email text, the document checklist, the tracking log template, and a brief note confirming this step now requires periodic follow-up with the attorney until their written clearance opinion is received.

legal_002:n5.prompt:
You are helping me prepare my trademark application for filing through {{vendor}}, the government trademark-filing service. The application covers my company name and/or logo. You will prepare everything, and I will make the sworn declaration and submit the filing myself.

First, ask me for anything missing:
- The exact mark (standard-character text and/or the logo image file).
- The legal applicant name, entity type, state of formation, and address.
- The goods and services I offer, in plain words.
- Whether the mark is already in use in commerce. If it is, ask for the first-use dates and a specimen, such as a screenshot or product photo. If it is not, I will file on an intent-to-use basis.
- The name and title of the authorized signer.

Then do the following:
1. Read {{vendor}}'s published guidance. Summarize the account, credential, and identity-verification steps that must be completed before filing. Flag any step a human must complete, such as multi-factor sign-in. If an account session is needed, use your configured credentials.
2. Look up the current filing fees per class on {{vendor}}'s own fee pages. Calculate my total.
3. Draft the identification of goods/services and suggest the correct class or classes, using {{vendor}}'s plain-language explainers. Note any wording that looks likely to draw an examiner's objection.
4. Open the online application form. Pre-fill every field you can from my answers and attach the mark and specimen files. Do not complete the signature or declaration section. Do not pay, and do not submit.
5. Note {{vendor}}'s published processing times and how I can check application status afterward.

Once the draft is fully prepared, stop for human sign-off. The declaration under penalty of perjury and the final submission must be done by the authorized signer, not by you.

Report back with:
- A checklist of pre-filled values.
- The class list with fees and the total cost.
- Any open questions or risks.
- Exactly where in the form I should resume to sign and submit.
- The expected processing time and how to check status.

legal_002:n6.prompt:
You are helping me track the status of a trademark application I filed with the USPTO for my company name and/or logo. This is an async, ongoing monitoring task since USPTO status updates arrive over weeks or months.

First, ask me for any of the following if you don't already have them: the USPTO serial number assigned to my application, the trademark owner name used on the filing, and my preferred email or notification method for status updates.

Then do the following:
1. Check the current status of my application using the USPTO's public trademark status and document retrieval tool (TSDR), searching by the serial number I provide.
2. Record the current status, the date of the last status change, and any upcoming deadlines (e.g., response due dates for office actions).
3. Note whether an Office Action, Notice of Allowance, or other examiner communication is pending or has been issued, and summarize what it requires if so.
4. Check whether I'm enrolled in the USPTO's free Trademark Trial and Appeal Board/status email alert service (TSDR email alerts or similar); if not, prepare the enrollment details (serial number, email) for me to submit myself, since account creation and confirmation on USPTO systems remains a human step.
5. Set up a recurring check-in cadence (e.g., note that you should re-poll status every 2-4 weeks, or immediately if I ask) and log each check's date and result so I have a running history.

When done, report back: the current official status, the last update date, any deadlines or required actions with their due dates, and a plain-language summary of what (if anything) I need to do next. Flag clearly if a response deadline is approaching so I don't miss it. If the application requires me to submit a legal response or pay a fee, prepare a draft summary of what's needed but do not submit anything on my behalf — that remains a human step.
